1.8.2 Cumulative distribution function of sum of independents
Theorem: Let X and Y be two independent (→ I/1.3.6) random variables (→ I/1.2.2) and let
Z = X + Y . Then, the cumulative distribution function (→ I/1.8.1) of Z is given by
FZ(z) = E [FX(z − Y )]
or FZ(z) = E [FY (z − X)] (1)
where FX(x), FY (y) and FZ(z) are the cumulative distribution functions (→ I/1.8.1) of X, Y and Z
and E [·] denotes the expected value (→ I/1.10.1).
Proof: Using the definition of the cumulative distribution function (→ I/1.8.1), the first equation
can be derived as follows:
FZ(z) = Pr(Z ≤ z)
= Pr(X + Y ≤ z)
= Pr(X ≤ z − Y )
= E [Pr(X ≤ z − Y |Y = y)]
= E [Pr(X ≤ z − Y )]
= E [FX(z − Y )] .
(2)
Note that the second-last transition is justified by the fact that X and Y are independent (→
I/1.3.6), such that conditional probabilities are equal to marginal probabilities (→ I/1.3.9). The
second equation can be derived by switching X and Y .

1.8.7 Exceedance probability based on cumulative distribution function
Theorem: Let X be a random variable (→ I/1.2.2) with possible values X and cumulative distri￾bution function (→ I/1.8.1) FX(x). Then, the exceedance probability (→ I/1.3.11) that X is larger
than some value x is
Pr(X > x) = 1 − FX(x) . (1)
Proof: Note that {X | X > x} and {X | X ≤ x} are disjoint sets
{X | X > x} ∩ {X | X ≤ x} = ∅ (2)
and that they comprise the set of all outcomes, i.e. the sample space (→ I/1.1.2):
{X | X > x} ∪ {X | X ≤ x} = X = Ω . (3)
Using the second axiom of probability (→ I/1.4.1), we have:
P(Ω) = 1
P ({X | X > x} ∪ {X | X ≤ x}) = 1 .
(4)
Using the third axiom of probability (→ I/1.4.1), we get:
P ({X | X > x}) + P ({X | X ≤ x}) = 1
P ({X | X > x}) = 1 − P ({X | X ≤ x})
Pr(X > x) = 1 − Pr(X ≤ x) .
(5)
Using the definition of the cumulative distribution function (→ I/1.8.1), we finally have:
Pr(X > x) = 1 − FX(x) . (6)

1.13.8 Law of total covariance
Theorem: (law of total covariance, also called “conditional covariance formula”) Let X, Y and Z
be random variables (→ I/1.2.2) defined on the same probability space (→ I/1.1.4) and assume that
the covariance (→ I/1.13.1) of X and Y is finite. Then, the sum of the expectation (→ I/1.10.1) of
the conditional covariance and the covariance (→ I/1.13.1) of the conditional expectations of X and
Y given Z is equal to the covariance (→ I/1.13.1) of X and Y :
Cov(X, Y ) = E[Cov(X, Y |Z)] + Cov[E(X|Z), E(Y |Z)] . (1)
Proof: The covariance can be decomposed into expected values (→ I/1.13.3) as follows:
Cov(X, Y ) = E(XY ) − E(X)E(Y ) . (2)
Then, conditioning on Z and applying the law of total expectation (→ I/1.10.12), we have:
Cov(X, Y ) = E [E(XY |Z)] − E [E(X|Z)] E [E(Y |Z)] . (3)
Applying the decomposition of covariance into expected values (→ I/1.13.3) to the first term gives:
Cov(X, Y ) = E [Cov(X, Y |Z) + E(X|Z)E(Y |Z)] − E [E(X|Z)] E [E(Y |Z)] . (4)
With the linearity of the expected value (→ I/1.10.5), the terms can be regrouped to give:
Cov(X, Y ) = E [Cov(X, Y |Z)] + (E [E(X|Z)E(Y |Z)] − E [E(X|Z)] E [E(Y |Z)]) . (5)
Once more using the decomposition of covariance into expected values (→ I/1.13.3), we finally have:
Cov(X, Y ) = E[Cov(X, Y |Z)] + Cov[E(X|Z), E(Y |Z)] . (6)
